<!-- Generated by toolkit/generator/generate.py from Prep Cook at 935ce00 (bug:planning playbook; product profile "Pantry" from docs/examples/scripts.toml). Edit freely: a good edit is a proposal — open a pull request, and once it becomes a playbook change the next regeneration carries it. A regeneration overwrites this file. -->

This picks up where `/prepcook-repro` stopped: `.repro/<KEY>/` holds a harness that fails on `<target>` and a `NOTES.md` with the commit and the UTC time of the run. Read its JSON lines and screenshots before reading code. The app is still up from `.prepcook/scripts.toml`, with the login in the environment, as `/prepcook-repro` checked.

The RCA is written to `docs/specs/<KEY>.html` on a branch named `<KEY>-rca` (created from `<target>` if it does not exist), posted to the ticket through your tracker's MCP, and filed in the Prep Cook knowledge store with the `kb_file_document` tool of the `prepcook` MCP — that is how it joins the graph of past RCAs. Read two or three neighbours first with `kb_list_documents` (kind `rca`) and `kb_get_document`: the same root-cause class may already be named. Outside a Prep Cook workspace the `prepcook` MCP cannot tell which board you mean; when a tool asks for a `project_id`, take it from `list_projects`.

`<target>` is the branch the work merges into: the target of the branch's pull request when one exists (ask `gh` or `glab`, whichever your host uses), else the remote's default branch — `git symbolic-ref --short refs/remotes/origin/HEAD`, usually `origin/main`. "Pull request" means a merge request too, on GitLab.

With the failure in hand — the harness under `.repro/<KEY>/` fails on `<target>`; if it does not, run `/prepcook-repro` first — find the mechanism: the code path the harness exercises, confirmed where possible by making the harness pass against a candidate change (rebuild and restart the app after the edit), not by reading alone. The app writes one JSON line per request and per error to logs/app.log in the worktree; read it (tail, grep or jq) for the stack trace and the request that caused a failure. There is no production log access. The harness is the local evidence. Assess the blast radius. Propose the fix as the smallest change that achieves the observed behaviour, and name the mechanism rather than the file — "the hook that validates a seeded value", not a filename — because the file you would name may not be the one the customer's path goes through. Then the regression tests that would have caught it.

Write the RCA as a single self-contained HTML document at docs/specs/<KEY>.html in this worktree (inline CSS/JS, no external assets; keep it LEAN — one short style block, default fonts, no JS) with sections: Symptom, Reproduction (the harness's source itself, HTML-escaped in a <pre> block and read through first for anything that looks like a credential, then its cases with expected and observed values, the UTC time and the commit the app was built from, the screenshots), Root cause (with evidence), Blast radius, Proposed fix, Regression tests, Open questions, and Reproduce locally: what the harness relied on from the seed (which seeded records, which user), and the kickoff prompt for a local session with the `prepcook-repro` skill, in the shape the repro-harness skill gives under Handing the reproduction on, with the prompt in a <pre> block the reader copies whole and no credential anywhere in either.

Post the reproduction on the ticket as soon as you have it, through your tracker's MCP (for Jira, `addCommentToJiraIssue`): `REPRODUCTION:` alone as the first line, then the harness's JSON lines, the mechanism in one paragraph, and "the app at `<target>`" with the commit and the UTC time — plain enough for the reporter, and the acceptance test `/prepcook-review` reads before it judges the branch; a reproduction it cannot find is reported as a missing one. Screenshots are attached to the ticket, never committed. Any question the harness cannot answer goes to the reporter in that comment.

When the RCA is done, record your verdict at the top of the document: kind (rca), open questions, confidence (low|medium|high), summary. If your confidence is below high, list concrete next steps that would raise confidence. Whenever there are open questions, record the ask as well: the audience — reporter or engineer — and the request itself, written in the words of whoever has to act on it. Choose the audience by who could actually do something about it. The root cause of a failure is an engineering question however badly a customer wants it answered, and putting one to the reporter parks the ticket on somebody who cannot move it while they work out it was never theirs. Record both or neither. Also write the client summary: the same outcome in 3-4 short sentences an account manager can send to a customer — what went wrong, who or what was affected, what the fix changes, and whether anyone needs to do anything. No jargon, no file or class names, no ticket numbers; if you cannot say it without them, say it more simply. Post it on the ticket when the RCA is done — it is the comment an account manager forwards, so write it for someone who will never open the RCA — and file the RCA in the knowledge store with the `prepcook` MCP's `kb_file_document` (kind rca, the ticket key, work_class bug, the summary, the document's HTML as the body); the orchestrator's graph analyst links it into the graph from there.

Stop here and hand the RCA to its reader. Feedback applies to the document AND to your analysis: update the verdict if it changes. Do not start the fix: `/prepcook-fix` is the next step, once you or a reviewer accept the RCA.

Tooling — prefer executing a repro over reasoning it out: use the project's own toolchain from the worktree (run failing paths and unit tests directly), Playwright with its bundled Chromium for UI checks (`npx playwright install chromium` once; `$PREPCOOK_CHROMIUM_PATH` when set), and `ffmpeg`, if present, to pull keyframes from downloaded ticket recordings. Treat any helper script you did not write as a black box: run it with `--help` rather than reading it into context. When you record confidence below high, add one sentence naming the missing confirmation, and make the single most valuable unanswered question the FIRST line of the next steps in the summary, phrased as a direct question to the team.
